# Exposed-face excision and all-circuit protection

This note adds a removed-mass localization to the exact quantile covers in
`candidate a0fdd477aa859374`. That archive already contains the
general first-order inverse-budget condition, including owner ties and
coincident cap facets. The new content here is its explicit local deletion
law, a pointwise exposed-set protection condition, a treatment of cap
boundaries through a deleted polytope vertex, and exact trim examples.
There is no claimed implication from a below-target depth to a profitable
exposed trim.

## 1. Actual fibers and critical circuits

Let P be a finite base set and let K_p be positive d-dimensional compact
convex fibers which are actual sections of C=conv union_p({p}×K_p).
Use mu=sum_p vol_d, M=mu(C)>0, and let beta be the maximum normalized
closed-halfspace depth on these fibers. Let I be the nonempty finite set
of bases attaining this maximum. Write Q=beta M.

A critical circuit at p in I consists of finitely many actual caps

    H_j={ (q,x): v_j.q+u_j.x>=b_j }, |u_j|=1,

of mass Q, through a maximizing point (p,y) in the interior of K_p,
and positive numbers rho_j with

    sum_j rho_j u_j=0.

The exact critical-cap lemmas proved in
`candidate b989614dc4f86228` supply such circuits. Only
a finite selected circuit is used in each argument below. No finite
representation of the full depth function or unique maximizing point is
assumed.

Two details remove possible boundary ambiguities. First, an active
containing cap can be moved parallel through its candidate: its mass cannot
fall below the depth infimum, so an originally active cap retains exactly
the same mass. Second, vertical caps are never active in a finite family
of positive full-dimensional fibers. Tighten a vertical cap through p and
partition the bases by the positive, zero, and negative signs of v.(q−p).
Let the first two total masses be M_+ and M_0; M_0>0 includes K_p.
For any nonzero continuous u and sufficiently large finite L, the two caps

    L v.(q−p) ± u.(x−y)>=0

include all positive-sign fibers, exclude all negative-sign fibers, and
partition the zero-sign fibers up to null continuous hyperplanes. Their
masses sum to 2M_++M_0, so one has mass at most M_++M_0/2, strictly less
than the vertical cap's M_++M_0. Both contain the candidate. Compact fibers
and a finite base make L finite. Entire boundary fibers have been counted,
not discarded.

Every circuit covers the entire continuous plane over its anchor base.
Indeed its weighted margins there sum identically to

    sum_j rho_j(v_j.p+u_j.x−b_j)=0.

At least one closed margin is nonnegative at every x. After changing only
thresholds, the same cover holds whenever

    sum_j rho_j(new b_j−b_j)<=0.                         (1)

## 2. An exact deletion criterion, including every coincidence

Let C_t be any feasible inner deformation with positive actual fibers,
mu_t=mu restricted to C_t, and epsilon_t=M−mu_t(C_t)>0 tending to zero.
Assume the chosen anchor interior balls persist. This holds for the exposed
trims below. For a selected cap write F_j(b)=mu(H_j(b)) and
F_j^t(b)=mu_t(H_j(b)). Near b_j, the unchanged anchor ball gives a uniform
positive lower slope for decreasing cap mass as the threshold increases.
The finite-fiber slab bound gives a uniform upper slope. Consequently the
nearby quantile b_j^t(tau), defined by F_j^t(b_j^t(tau))=tau, exists uniquely
and continuously for tau near Q. Its shift is O(epsilon_t) when
tau=Q−beta epsilon_t. These assertions follow also directly from the
monotone inverse proof in the quantile-cover archive.

For one selected circuit at each deepest base, put

    E_p(t)=sum_j rho_j[b_j^t(Q−beta epsilon_t)−b_j].     (2)

**Exact criterion.** If E_p(t)<0 for every selected deepest-base circuit,
then the new maximum depth is strictly less than beta for all sufficiently
small such t.

Proof: continuity permits lowering the common mass Q−beta epsilon_t by
a small positive amount in each circuit while keeping its weighted
threshold shift nonpositive. Equation (1) still covers every point over
that base, and all covering caps have mass strictly below
beta(M−epsilon_t). The finitely many nondeep bases have strict original
depth gaps; retain their original circuit covers. Shrinking the body cannot
increase these fixed cap masses, and their gaps persist as epsilon_t->0.
All candidate points in every new actual fiber are therefore covered by
a cap of mass strictly below beta(M−epsilon_t). This proves the claim.

This criterion does not linearize any coincident facet or omit cap-boundary
mass. It applies even when the derivative formulas below are unavailable.

## 3. Localized deletion and the two threshold slopes

For each original critical cap define

    S_j^+ = total proper-section area
            + total supporting-facet area in fibers INSIDE H_j,
    S_j^- = total proper-section area
            + total supporting-facet area in fibers OUTSIDE H_j.

Section areas use H_(d−1), with unit continuous normal. Lower-dimensional
supporting sections contribute zero; in d=1 use H_0 on endpoints. The
anchor's proper section makes both slopes strictly positive. Coarea and
the one-sided section limits of a convex body give

    F_j(b_j+s)=Q−S_j^+ s+o(|s|),    s down to 0,
    F_j(b_j+s)=Q−S_j^- s+o(|s|),    s up to 0.            (3)

At a proper section the density is continuous. At a supporting facet its
inner one-sided section areas converge to the facet area and its outer
ones vanish. The inner convergence follows from convex interpolation with
an interior point for a lower bound and compactness for an upper bound.
Thus (3) also holds for nonpolytopal convex fibers.

Let R_t=C\C_t, understood with its mixed measure, and suppose along the
chosen t-sequence that

    mu(R_t intersect H_j)/epsilon_t -> iota_j in [0,1],
    mu(R_t intersect {|v_j.q+u_j.x−b_j|<=A epsilon_t})
                                        =o(epsilon_t)  (4)

for every fixed A and every selected cap. The second condition retains
the interaction between moving a cap and deleting material. It must not
be silently omitted.

The quantile shift is O(epsilon_t). Equation (4) permits replacing the
deleted cap mass at that shifted threshold by epsilon_t iota_j+o(epsilon_t).
Using (3) in its quantile equation gives

    [b_j^t(Q−beta epsilon_t)−b_j]/epsilon_t ->
       (beta−iota_j)_+/S_j^+
          −(iota_j−beta)_+/S_j^-.                        (5)

If iota_j=beta, the inverse lower slope makes the limit zero. The other
two signs choose the displayed right or left slope; this is exactly where
coincident supporting facets matter.

Define the circuit deletion response

    Phi_C(iota)=sum_j rho_j [
          (beta−iota_j)_+/S_j^+
             −(iota_j−beta)_+/S_j^- ].                    (6)

If one circuit at each deepest base has Phi_C<0, then (2) is strictly
negative for all sufficiently small terms of the sequence, and the exact
criterion proves full maximum-depth descent. This controls all maximizing
centers by an actual whole-fiber cover.

For transverse cuts, S_j^+=S_j^-=S_j and (6) is negative exactly when

    sigma_C(iota):=
       [sum_j (rho_j/S_j)iota_j]/[sum_j rho_j/S_j] > beta. (7)

For binary incidences iota_j=I_j in {0,1}, the exact nonsmooth analogue is

    sigma_C^ns(I)=
      [sum_(I_j=1)rho_j/S_j^-]
      /[sum_(I_j=1)rho_j/S_j^-+sum_(I_j=0)rho_j/S_j^+].    (8)

Its denominator is positive. Equation (6) is negative precisely when
sigma_C^ns(I)>beta. Using a convenient common section slope instead of
these two actual slopes would be unjustified.

## 4. One supporting-plane trim and pointwise protection

Let ell be an ambient affine functional with maximum h on C and exposed
face F={ell=h} intersect C. Set C_t=C intersect {ell<=h−t}. For small t,
all original positive fibers remain positive whenever their exposed
sections are proper boundary faces; there are finitely many fibers.
The new fibers are actual sections of one convex body, so compatibility
is exact. An interior ball away from the supporting plane survives.
The fibers converge back in Hausdorff distance as t decreases to zero:
interpolation with one interior point below the cutting plane approximates
every original boundary point. Thus these trims are local competitors in
the attained problem, not merely inclusions with the right measured mass.

If F is disjoint from every selected cap boundary, convexity and
connectedness make its cap incidence constant I_j=0 or 1. Compactness
implies R_t approaches F. Hence for small t its incidence remains I_j,
even after every threshold shift of size O(epsilon_t); (4) holds with
zero interaction. Provided epsilon_t>0, (8) is an exact local deletion
test in every dimension d>=1. The face need not be a single point.

In particular let v=(p0,x0) be an exposed point belonging to the measured
source. Its exposing functional has nonzero continuous component, since
K_p0 has interior. The finite other fibers have a strict support gap,
so for sufficiently small t ONLY K_p0 is trimmed. Its removed cap has
positive d-volume. This is a legitimate actual one-fiber deletion without
any compatibility repair.

Suppose the original family is an unrestricted local depth minimum among
positive actual families on P. For every such v, let C_p(v) be all critical
circuits at the deepest base p whose cap boundaries avoid v. Then

    there exists p in I such that
       sigma_C^ns(v)<=beta for EVERY C in C_p(v).          (9)

The quantifiers are important. If (9) failed, at each of the finitely many
deepest bases choose one circuit with sigma_C^ns(v)>beta. This finite
selection has a common cap-boundary gap around v, and the same exposed
trim satisfies the strict deletion criterion simultaneously. Conversely,
the inability to select a strict circuit at every base is exactly (9).
If C_p(v) is empty, its universal statement is vacuous; no assertion about
a boundary-passing circuit is hidden in this formulation. In the transverse
case use (7) instead of (8).

An unrestricted attained minimum is available under the conditional
counterexample reduction in `candidate c280bb0dcfd30f3d`,
Sections 4--8. A minimum only in its fixed N-plane subclass, Section 9,
does NOT automatically permit adding a new supporting plane. At that
restricted minimum this necessary condition is valid only for trims staying
in its allowed class, for example offsets of an already included plane.

## 5. Boundary-passing caps at an exposed polytope vertex

There is a complete version of (9) for an exposed polytope vertex when
d>=2, with no requirement that selected caps avoid that vertex.
Only its base p0 is trimmed. Translate its vertex to zero and let W be
the tangent cone of K_p0 there. The exposing continuous functional is
strictly negative on every nonzero cone ray. The set

    B={w in W: −ell_cont(w)<=1}

is therefore a bounded full-dimensional truncated cone. For all sufficiently
small t, the removed set, up to its null boundary, is exactly tB: nonincident
polytope facets have a fixed positive gap, and all incident ones define W.
Consequently epsilon_t=t^d |B|. A cap strictly containing or excluding the
vertex has iota_j=1 or 0. A cap through the vertex has the exact incidence

    iota_j=|B intersect {u_j.w>=0}|/|B|.                  (10)

These limits exist without any choice of subsequence. The moving-threshold
interaction in (4) is o(epsilon_t): the removed region has diameter O(t),
so its intersection with a slab of width O(epsilon_t) has volume at most
O(epsilon_t t^(d−1))=o(epsilon_t). This uses d>=2. It includes all
orientations of the selected ambient caps and all supporting coincidences
in other fibers.

Thus at an unrestricted polytopal local minimum, for EVERY exposed vertex
and EVERY exposing functional there is a deepest base p such that EVERY
critical circuit there has Phi_C(iota)>=0, using (6) and (10). The same
finite-selection negation argument proves this universal statement. It
applies in a fixed-complexity class only under the admissibility condition
in Section 4. For d=1, the slab interaction need not be lower order; retain
the exact quantile criterion (2) rather than asserting (10) is sufficient.

For arbitrary convex exposed points in d>=2, the same interaction estimate
holds with the diameter tending to zero; finite incidence vectors always
have subsequential limits. Formula (6) therefore applies along every such
common subsequence. No uniqueness of a tangent cone or incidence limit is
assumed in that nonpolytopal case.

## 6. Exact corner deletion undetected by every first variation

In d=2 let

    K_t=[−1,1]^2 intersect {x+y<=2−t},  0<=t<=1.

This moves one already included supporting plane; at t=0 it touches a
vertex and is redundant. The removed triangle has area epsilon=t²/2,
so every fixed cap's first variation in t is zero. Total variation and
the unchanged original center also make the first variation of maximum
depth zero.

At t=0 the square's center has depth beta=1/2. Select its critical circuit
with normals (1,0),(0,1),(−1,−1)/sqrt(2) and weights (1,1,sqrt(2)).
The section lengths are 2,2,2sqrt(2), so its normalized reciprocal-section
weights are all 1/3. The removed vertex belongs to the first two caps and
not the third: sigma=2/3>1/2. Thus the removed-mass test sees strict descent
even though every first variation in the plane-offset parameter vanishes.

Here is a finite exact certificate. The three caps

    x>=−t²/12,       y>=−t²/12,       x+y<=−t²/6

cover the entire plane: if the first two fail, the third holds. Their
K_t areas are respectively

    2−t²/3,    2−t²/3,    2−t²/3+t^4/72.

For the first two, enlarge the corresponding half-square by area t²/6
and subtract the whole removed triangle. For the third, the square sum
section gives area 2−2h+h²/2 with h=t²/6, and the deleted corner is
disjoint from it. Therefore

    D(K_t)<= [2−t²/3+t^4/72]/[4−t²/2]
       =1/2− t²(6−t²)/[72(4−t²/2)] <1/2.                (11)

Products with [−1,1]^(d−2) give this example for every d>=2. Products also
with the integer box [−1,1]^n give actual full-dimensional mixed bodies
whose 3^n fibers all have equal mass, strictly less than M/2^n when n>=1.
The same three cylindrical caps cover every candidate at every base, so
(11) bounds the complete mixed maximum as well. At t=0 the maximum is
1/2 at base zero and continuous center zero, by symmetry. Every nonzero
integer base has a coordinate at an endpoint; a finite tilt isolates that
coordinate layer and a continuous median cap gives depth at most 1/6.
Thus base zero is uniquely deepest initially. For n>0 or d>2 the moved
plane exposes a face, rather than a single ambient point; its cap signs
are nevertheless constant, exactly as required in Section 4.

## 7. A no-heavy obstruction to universal single-point trimming

Fix n>=2,d>=2 and any full-dimensional rectangular box Q centered at zero.
Take

    C=[−1,1]×[0,1]^(n−1)×Q.

There are 3·2^(n−1) equal positive fibers. Every mass is strictly less
than M/2^n, and every fiber has positive ordinary and paired deficit
because D(Q)=D_pair(Q)=1/2>Gamma_d.
For the ordinary equality use central symmetry for the lower bound and a
continuous coordinate median cap for the upper bound. For the paired
equality every centered projection is continuous and symmetric, so its
opposite-shift tails sum to one; the zero-shift ordinary upper bound
then gives equality.

Write eta for the binary vector in {0,1}^(n−1). Each eta-layer consists
of three identical Q fibers at bases −1,0,1. Its own maximum absolute
depth is 3|Q|/2: its central candidate has this depth by symmetry, and a
continuous coordinate cap bounds every candidate by it. Each binary
vertex layer can be isolated by a finite integer tilt without changing
its internal caps. Thus the full source has exactly

    D(C intersect Lambda)= [3|Q|/2]/[3·2^(n−1)|Q|]=2^(−n).

Every ambient exposed point is a product vertex. A sufficiently small
supporting-plane trim exposing just that point changes exactly one integer
base and hence only one eta-layer. Another eta-layer exists because n>=2.
It is unchanged and retains a candidate whose EVERY containing ambient
halfspace receives at least 3|Q|/2 from that layer alone. The total mass
has strictly fallen, so the full maximum depth strictly INCREASES.

This holds for every sufficiently small single-point exposed trim, despite
positive ordinary/paired deficits and absence of heavy fibers. It does not
contradict a below-target assertion: its depth 2^(−n) is larger than
Gamma_d/2^n. It shows why that numerical hypothesis, or a trim affecting
several protected layers, cannot be omitted from a future argument.

## 8. Exact remaining gap

The exposed-point protection law is a necessary local condition, and (11)
is a certified useful case of its failure. No proof has been supplied that
an attained family with beta<Gamma_d/h(P), or below the OC target, must
admit an exposed point or exposed face violating every required protection
condition simultaneously. The no-heavy example above prevents promoting
ordinary/paired nonsimplicity and local stationarity alone into that claim.
The summed-deficit compatibility-cost bridge remains closed by the earlier
all-dimensional obstruction and is not used anywhere in this note.

## 9. Exact regression verification

`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_exposed_face_excision_and_protection.py` uses rational polygon
clipping and the shoelace formula to check all three explicit cap areas,
the exact depth decrement, and the actual six-base isolated-point trim.
It also checks the all-dimensional layer masses and the two-slope
incidence identity. Output:

    PASS: 187 exact corner-cap and six-base trims;
    324 all-dimensional no-heavy protected-layer cases;
    32 nonsmooth incidence identities.

These finite checks supplement the general proofs and do not substitute
for the quantified descent or protection statements.
